name: Ruy López Closed Variation
summary: The Closed Ruy López reaches the main Spanish tabiya where Black holds e5 with ...d6 and White prepares d4 and Nb1-d2-f1-g3.
intro: The Closed Variation is the heart of the Ruy López, reached after 3...a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O. Black keeps the pawn chain intact and holds firmly to the e5-square rather than releasing the central tension, inviting a long, deep manoeuvring battle. White readies the central break d4 and the famous knight tour Nb1-d2-f1-g3, while Black regroups his own pieces to defend e5 and generate counterplay. From this single tabiya branch the great named systems - Breyer, Chigorin, Zaitsev, Smyslov and more - each a lifetime study in its own right. It is the purest expression of what commentators call the Spanish torture.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining feature of the Closed Ruy López is the maintained tension between White's e4-pawn and Black's e5-pawn, with White's coming d4 hanging over the position for many moves. Rather than resolving the centre early, both sides complete a slow, careful build-up: White plays h3 to prevent an annoying ...Bg4 pin, prepares d4, and only then decides when to release or maintain the tension. Because the pawn structure stays fluid, the middlegame is dominated by piece manoeuvring and prophylaxis, and small inaccuracies in placement tell over the long term. This grinding, positional character is why the Closed Spanish is regarded as one of the deepest strategic battlegrounds in all of chess.

White's signature idea is the knight regrouping Nb1-d2-f1-g3, redeploying the queen's knight toward the kingside where it eyes f5 and supports a build-up against Black's king. In tandem, White often plays Bc2 to tuck the light-squared bishop behind the e4-pawn, adding a second attacker along the b1-h7 diagonal and reinforcing the centre. Black meanwhile must decide how to treat the tension on e5: capturing on d4 concedes the centre, so Black usually keeps the pawn defended and looks for queenside expansion or a timely ...d5 break. The result is a rich strategic duel where control of the central squares and the fate of the e5-pawn shape every plan.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: From the tabiya after 8...O-O, White most often continues 9.h3, and Black chooses among a family of famous regrouping systems named after the players who developed them. The Breyer Variation retreats the knight with 9...Nb8, intending ...Nbd7 to reinforce e5 and free the c-pawn, a paradoxical but deeply respected plan. The Chigorin Variation plays 9...Na5 to hit the b3-bishop and expand with ...c5 on the queenside, the classical main line for much of the twentieth century. The Zaitsev Variation with 9...Bb7 and ...Re8 pressures e4 directly and became a favourite of Karpov, while the Smyslov and Karpov systems offer their own subtle move orders for regrouping behind the e5-pawn.

Two important early deviations shape which of these systems Black can reach. Instead of the slow 8...O-O, Black can seize the initiative with the Marshall Attack, sacrificing a pawn after ...O-O and ...d5 for a powerful kingside attack, which forces White to prepare a specific antidote or dodge into an Anti-Marshall. White too has choices: the Worrall Attack substitutes Qe2 for Re1, and the Centre Attack strikes with an early d4 rather than the patient c3 build-up. Within the Closed itself, the maintained e5-versus-d4 tension and the choice of when White finally plays d4 or dxe5 remain the recurring strategic crossroads.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Closed Ruy López rose to prominence as classical opening theory matured in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and it became the proving ground on which generations of World Champions tested their positional understanding. Its slow, accumulating pressure earned the whole opening the nickname the Spanish torture, and the Closed lines embody that reputation most fully. Players such as Capablanca, Keres and Smyslov refined the manoeuvring plans, and the opening remained a central battleground in World Championship play throughout the era of classical chess.

In the second half of the twentieth century the Closed Spanish reached its theoretical peak, driven above all by the epic Karpov-Kasparov World Championship matches, where the Zaitsev and Chigorin systems were analysed to extraordinary depth. Anatoly Karpov made the Zaitsev a personal weapon, while the Breyer earned a reputation as an exceptionally solid choice at the highest level. Even in the modern era of engines and sharp gambit alternatives, the Closed Ruy López endures as a benchmark of strategic chess, studied by ambitious players precisely because its slow richness rewards deep understanding.

keyIdeas: The maintained e5-versus-d4 tension defines the slow Spanish torture.
White regroups with the classic knight tour Nb1-d2-f1-g3 toward the kingside.
Bc2 tucks the bishop behind e4, reinforcing the centre and the b1-h7 diagonal.
h3 first prevents the ...Bg4 pin before White commits to d4.
Black holds e5 with ...d6 and chooses a named regrouping system.
Breyer, Chigorin, Zaitsev and Smyslov all branch from this one tabiya.

white: Play h3 to stop ...Bg4, then prepare the central break d4.
Reroute the queen's knight via d2-f1-g3 toward f5 and the kingside.
Redeploy the bishop to c2 to reinforce e4 and eye Black's king.
Decide when to maintain, advance, or exchange the d4 tension favourably.
Build slowly and increase pressure across the whole board over time.
black: Hold the e5-pawn with ...d6 rather than releasing the central tension.
Choose a regrouping system: Breyer's ...Nb8-d7, Chigorin's ...Na5, or Zaitsev's ...Bb7.
Expand on the queenside with ...c5 to gain space and counterplay.
Prepare the freeing ...d5 break when the pieces are ready to support it.
Contest e4 directly with ...Bb7 and ...Re8 to keep White's centre under fire.
